quick_notes.title: Periyar E.V. Ramasamy
quick_notes.detail: Founder of Self-Respect Movement (1925). Known as "Thanthai Periyar". Fought against caste and for women's rights.
quick_notes.explanation: Periyar E.V. Ramasamy was a social reformer from Tamil Nadu, India who lived from 1879 to 1973. In 1925, he founded the Self-Respect Movement, which was a campaign to encourage people to value themselves and reject unfair social rules based on caste. Caste is a traditional Hindu system that divides people into fixed groups by birth, often causing unequal treatment and discrimination. Periyar is commonly called "Thanthai Periyar," where Thanthai means "father" in Tamil, to show his

quick_notes.title: Vaikom Satyagraha (1924)
quick_notes.detail: Fought for the right of untouchables to walk on roads near Vaikom temple (Kerala). Periyar's leadership earned him the title "Vaikom Veerar".
quick_notes.explanation: Vaikom Satyagraha (1924) was a non-violent protest in Vaikom, Kerala, where people from the lowest social group, called "untouchables" (a term for those considered outside the caste system), were banned from walking on the roads surrounding the Vaikom Mahadeva Temple. The protest demanded that these roads be opened to everyone, regardless of caste. E. V. Ramasamy, popularly known as Periyar, led the movement, and his courageous role earned him the title "Vaikom Veerar," which means "Hero of Vaikom." The protest lasted over a year and eventually succeeded in partially opening the roads to all people, marking an early victory for social equality in India.

quick_notes.title: Self-Respect Movement
quick_notes.detail: Objectives: Removal of caste, Self-respect marriages (without Brahmin priests), Women empowerment. Slogan : "No God, No Religion, No Caste".
quick_notes.explanation: Self-Respect Movement was a social reform started in 1925 by E. V. Ramasamy, who is also known as Periyar. Its main goal was to remove the caste system, which is a system of social classes based on birth, because Periyar believed it kept people unequal. The movement promoted Self-Respect Marriages, which are weddings performed without a Brahmin priest (a priest from the highest Hindu caste) so that people from any background could marry without following upper-caste rules. It also worked for Women Empowerment, meaning giving women equal rights and freedom, like the choice to marry without asking anyone's permission. The slogan of the movement was "No God, No Religion, No Caste," which means the movement did not believe in any god, any organized religion, or any caste divisions.

quick_notes.title: Journals & Books
quick_notes.detail: Kudi Arasu (Main journal), Revolt, Puratchi, Viduthalai. Book : "Why Women were Enslaved?".
quick_notes.explanation: A journal is a magazine or newspaper published regularly on a specific topic. Kudi Arasu, meaning Republic, was the main journal started by the social reformer Periyar E. V. Ramasamy to spread ideas of rationalism and self-respect. Other journals he published were Revolt, an English-language paper, Puratchi meaning Revolution, and Viduthalai meaning Freedom. The book titled Why Women were Enslaved? is Periyar's work that argues how religious texts and social customs have historically oppressed women and kept them in a subordinate position. Each of these publications and the book were tools to challenge caste hierarchy, superstition, and gender inequality.

quick_notes.title: UNESCO Citation (1970)
quick_notes.detail: "Prophet of a New Age, Socrates of South East Asia".
quick_notes.explanation: UNESCO stands for the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, a special agency of the United Nations that works to protect world heritage and promote education and science. In 1970, UNESCO gave a special citation to the Indian philosopher and social reformer Thiruvalluvar, who wrote the ancient Tamil text called the Thirukkural. The citation called him the "Prophet of a New Age" and the "Socrates of South East Asia," meaning he was seen as a visionary teacher for modern times and was compared to the famous Greek philosopher Socrates for his wisdom and influence across the region. This recognition honored Thiruvalluvar's teachings on ethics, non-violence, and justice, which are still studied today. The citation is a formal statement of praise and acknowledgment from UNESCO, not a prize or award with money. It highlights how Thiruvalluvar's ideas are considered important for all of humanity, not just for India.
